articles.title: Woman, 100, Loves To Cycle and Is the Oldest Person at Her Gym. Her 4 Tips for a Long Life
articles.summary: Ellen Jones is the oldest person at her gym at 100 years old. The centenarian credits movement and a loving support system for her long and healthy life.
articles.body: “Shall I just start with my life?” Ellen Jones asks during her phone interview. At 100 years old, she doesn’t attribute her longevity to a single recipe, a trendy supplement or a strict routine. For her, the secret to a century of life lies in how you live it: staying curious, being active and building a loving community around you. Born on February 22, 1926, in Waterford, Michigan, Jones worked as the superintendent of schools’ secretary in Pontiac, Michigan, before having her first child. The decades that followed were spent playing various sports, traveling with her husband (they highly recommend Australia and Alaska!) and working on several of her church’s volunteer committees. Four children, nine grandchildren, nine great-grandchildren and one great-great-grandson later, Jones remains the matriarch for the family and its five generations. “They’ve kept me busy! I love to go to all of their games and so forth,” she tells TODAY.com. These days, Jones makes time for her family, reading, monthly bridge games and volunteering at the community center in Waterford. In light of her athletic days, Jones had also signed up for a gym membership at Crunch Fitness, consistently working out three to five times a week with exercises she says, “make all the difference.” Here are some of her mindful tips in leading a long life. Find Your Team Jones has been a lover of exercise for most of her life, from coaching elementary school softball teams to eventually trying her own hand in sports. She spent 40 years playing golf before pivoting to volleyball and playing for the Michigan Senior Olympic Volleyball Team, “Michigan Movers.” She was 69 years old when she started. “I loved volleyball,” Jones recalls, regarding it as her favorite sport she’s played. “I was a setter for a while...and then we had a new girl come in that was much better than I was,” she says, laughing. Jones was eventually made her team’s captain. In staying involved with her center’s team for nearly 30 years, Jones traveled with her team every few years for competitions across the U.S. and made friends she still keeps in contact with now, despite no longer playing. Now, she meets with her niece’s bridge group to play once a month, and stresses the importance of staying on your feet. “I try to keep as active as I can,” she added. Keep Moving When she developed neuropathy in her feet and underwent surgery on her knees that made it too difficult to continue volleyball, Jones took up a membership at Crunch Fitness. She attributes much of her good health to her “consistent” workouts, and hits the gym as often as “three to four times a week.” “I would recommend a stationary bicycle for 30 minutes. That made all the difference,” Jones says. “It’s the best thing for my knees.” Jones has incorporated that exercise into her routine for about ten years alongside her gym friends, a few workout partners in their “mid-80s” that “keep her young.” Outside of the gym, she also looks for opportunities to move throughout the day, whether that’s walking around her neighborhood or browsing at the mall with her daughters. “Mom will remind me, ‘We haven’t been out for a walk, we’ve got to go for a walk,’” Jones’ daughter Jill Underwood tells TODAY.com. “She motivates herself.” “Just don’t sit on your fanny day-in and day-out,” Jones instructs. Establish Healthy Eating Habits Jones’ healthy habits extend well past going to the gym. The centenarian also highlighted the importance of keeping a balanced diet. She often starts her mornings with yogurt and granola, and makes sure to include protein in her diet with a chicken salad sandwich or muffin with peanut butter for lunch. Jones also took pride in never smoking or being an avid coffee drinker throughout her life. “She’s a healthy eater,” her daughter says, adding that Jones is also consistent in taking her vitamins and drinking enough water. Stay Connected Above all, Jones attributes much of her good life to the family and friends she’s surrounded herself with day after day. “Everybody congregates around her,” says Underwood. “She gets the party going.” Jones hosted the family’s Thanksgiving and Christmas holiday dinners for most of her life. Even now, as she passes the torch to her daughters and granddaughters, she remains the “heart of the party” at family events, and feels blessed that she has a “wonderful family” to rely on. “Let them do all the work,” Jones says, laughing. In addition to family, Jones has maintained friendships across her community thanks to her church, her volleyball team and her friends at Crunch Fitness. “I’ve been at (my) church since 1957,” Jones says. The centenarian has remained a loyal member of its community throughout her life, “helping” in the church offices and working on various volunteer committees. At the gym, she’ll often strike up conversations with those around her, developing friendships with other regulars. “You have to find a place as friendly as (my) gym. I’ve been very, very fortunate,” says Jones. Jones was even able to celebrate her 90th and 100th birthdays at her local Crunch Fitness, in honor of being their only 100-year-old member. “It was really fun. I made a lot of good friends, and I’ve been blessed with having good friends and a wonderful family,” Jones says. “I don’t think you could ever ask for more than that.”

articles.title: Robert F Kennedy's granddaughter dies at 42 after years of health struggles
articles.summary: Kyle Kennedy, granddaughter of Bobby and Ethel Kennedy, was a Georgetown University graduate and Teach for America alumna who championed for education reform.
articles.body: Kyle Kennedy, the granddaughter of Robert F. Kennedy and Ethel Kennedy, has died at the age of 42. Kennedy, the daughter of Michael Kennedy and Victoria Gifford Kennedy, died Sept. 21 at her Massachusetts home, according to an obituary published by Burke Funeral Homes. Her cause of death remains pending, People reported. TATIANA SCHLOSSBERG, JFK'S GRANDDAUGHTER, DIES AT 35 AFTER YEAR-AND-A-HALF LEUKEMIA BATTLE Born in Washington, D.C., on July 6, 1984, Kennedy spent much of her upbringing in Cohasset, Massachusetts. She attended Milton Academy before earning a bachelor’s degree in history from Georgetown University. She went on to pursue advanced degrees in education, earning a master of science in early education from Pace University and a master of education in education policy and management from the Harvard Graduate School of Education. Kennedy began her professional life with Teach for America, teaching for two years in New York City public schools. That experience sparked a lifelong commitment to early childhood education and reform, according to her obituary. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER Over the course of her career, Kennedy worked as an advocate for equitable elementary education and charter schools, collaborated with education technology companies on curriculum improvement, and served as an instructional coach for primary school educators. An avid athlete and long-distance runner, Kennedy completed the 2019 Boston Marathon. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ In 2020, Kennedy suffered a severe spinal cord injury that caused long-term paralysis and significant health obstacles. Following her injury, Kennedy focused on disability rights advocacy, including testifying at the Massachusetts State House on healthcare discrimination against individuals living with disabilities. CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES Kennedy was preceded in death by her father, Michael, in 1997, and her infant daughter, Josie. Kennedy is survived by her sons, Conor, 12, and Declan, 10; her ex-husband, Liam; her mother, Victoria (the daughter of Frank Gifford and Maxine Avis Ewart and Kathie Lee Gifford’s stepdaughter); her brother, Michael, and his family; and her sister, Rory, and her family. articles.title: A Viral Video Claims Blowing Bubbles on the Toilet Can Help You Poop. A GI Doc Reveals If It’s True
articles.summary: In a viral video, a physical therapist said blowing bubbles can help you poop. A gastroenterologist weighed in on whether it really works and how to do it right.
articles.body: Constipation means you have difficulty passing stool — which can show up in a lot of different ways. Maybe you have fewer than three bowel movements a week, or they’re dry, hard and painful. Another sign is feeling like you never fully empty your intestines after going to the bathroom, according to the National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases. Because of the varied symptoms, finding relief won’t look the same for everyone either. Home constipation remedies are popular online, and a somewhat strange one recently went viral: blowing bubbles through a straw while sitting on the toilet. In the Instagram post, Kelly Peterson, doctor of physical therapy and pelvic rehabilitation practitioner, said the hack can help you poop without straining or pushing, sparing you from hemorrhoids, anal fissures, bloating, trapped gas and pelvic pain. As unconventional as it might sound, it’s actually worthy advice, an expert says. What Is Constipation? Constipation, whether chronic or temporary, is a digestive condition that makes it difficult to have a bowel movement. It can manifest in so many ways because constipation is specific to each individual, explains Dr. Olufemi Kassim, gastroenterologist and clinical assistant professor at Northwestern Medicine. While you may have learned that healthy gut means pooping once or twice per day, “you don’t actually need to,” Kassim tells TODAY.com. “There’s a big range in terms of … frequency. So, you can go anywhere from every three days to three times a day, (and that) can be normal as long as you feel comfortable.” Once you become familiar with your bathroom cadence, you’ll know when you’re constipated because your bowel movements will become difficult or painful, you’ll feel bloated, experience nausea, go less frequently than normal, or the consistency of your stool will change. But going fewer times than someone else doesn’t necessarily mean you’re constipated, and going more than someone doesn’t necessarily mean you aren’t. Causes for constipation range from certain medications, lack of fiber and a sedentary lifestyle to certain illnesses and conditions, including pregnancy, and blockages in the intestines. Breathing Exercises To Poop The group of muscles known as the pelvic floor controls your rectum and several other organs, says Kassim, so “the pelvic floor needs to be engaged in the right way to have bowel movements.” Breathing exercises, such as slowly exhaling while you blow bubbles, are a great way to activate those muscles for a bowel movement and develop the mind-to-muscle connection required to poop, she adds. The slow exhale required to blow bubbles is called a Valsalva maneuver. It’s what happens when you exhale against a closed airway. When you strain to poop, for example, you might to do the Valsalva maneuver by keeping your nose and mouth while blowing out air. But if you do this too often or for too long, you might damage your pelvic floor muscles or develop tears in your anal canal or hemorrhoids from pushing too hard. On the other hand, the Valsalva maneuver where you blow bubbles requires you not to use your nose and instead to blow air out of your mouth slowly and with control. Doing so engages your pelvic floor, increases abdominal pressure and allows you to push the stool out. There’s no need to take this too literally, however, says Kassim. While you can bring a drink and straw into the bathroom and blow bubbles if you’d like, you can just mimic the movement, too. Slowly push air out of only your mouth. The goal is “consistent exhalation,” Kassim says. You might even vocalize while you do it. For example, say A, E, I, O or U while you exhale, do it for five to 10 seconds, and then breathe normally, repeating as needed. Instead of blowing bubbles, you can also imagine blowing out a candle, Kassim adds. Put your hand on your lower belly while you do it, and you’ll feel the pressure in your abdominals taking effect. Other Remedies To Relieve Constipation When you’re struggling to have a bowel movement, Kassim says to adhere to the five-minute rule. “Sit on the toilet for five minutes. No distractions. No phone. No magazine. Don’t read the shampoo bottle. Just focus on having your bowel movement,” she says. “If it hasn’t happened in five minutes, it’s not your time, and you should just try again after your next meal.” Some of her other tips for successful bowel movement include: Eat enough fiber. Most Americans aren’t eating enough fiber. “You want to get 25-35 grams of dietary fiber daily,” Kassim says. Increase fruit, vegetable and whole grain intake. You can also take a fiber supplement, which you can get in capsule or gummy form.Stay hydrated. If you don’t drink enough water, all that fiber won’t do much. Water helps everything you consume flow through your digestive tract.Position yourself to support the angle of the rectum. An easy way to do this is to elevate your feet, says Kassim. While you’re sitting on the toilet, you might put your feet on a stool or a stack of books so that you’re in a squatting position, making for a straight path from your colon to your anus.Try medication. There are plenty of over-the-counter medications for constipation, including laxatives and stool softeners. Your doctor will advise you if you need them or recommend prescriptions if necessary. If your constipation is getting in the way of your everyday life or last longer than two to three weeks, it may be time to see a healthcare provider, according to Mayo Clinic.

articles.title: Ben Kindel in stable condition after “medical episode,” Penguins say
articles.summary: Penguins forward Ben Kindel is in stable condition after a “medical episode” on the flight back to Pittsburgh from Salt Lake City. The Penguins said Tuesday...
articles.body:
Penguins forward Ben Kindel is in stable condition after a "medical episode" on the flight back to Pittsburgh from Salt Lake City.

The Penguins said Tuesday afternoon that the team plane returned to Salt Lake City International Airport shortly after takeoff after Kindel had a medical episode. The nature of the incident wasn't detailed.

The team said that Dr. Dharmesh Vyas, the team physician, and other medical staff were onboard the plane, all of whom immediately attended to Kindel.

"An ambulance was waiting upon arrival, and he was taken to the University of Utah Hospital for further evaluation," the team said, adding that Kindel's condition was listed as "stable" and that he was conscious and alert.

The team said that the health and safety of players, along with their privacy, is the top priority and that further updates will be provided when appropriate.

Kindel, 19, is in his second season with the Penguins after playing 77 games as a rookie last year.

articles.title: Disabled Canadian man says hospital repeatedly offered assisted death as he fought for care to stay alive
articles.summary: Roger Foley told Fox News Digital that Ontario hospital staff repeatedly raised assisted dying while he fought for self-directed home care funding.
articles.body: A Canadian man battling a debilitating neurological disease told Fox News Digital that hospital staff repeatedly raised the possibility of medically assisted death while he was fighting for the home care he says he needs to survive. Roger Foley, who has spinocerebellar ataxia, told Fox News Digital in a recent interview that the conversations began in 2016 at Victoria Hospital, part of the London Health Sciences Centre in Ontario, where he says he has remained hospitalized for years while seeking a self-directed home-care arrangement. In a July 7, 2026, letter obtained by Fox News Digital, Foley's attending physician said he could safely leave the hospital if the Ontario government authorized an individualized home-care arrangement. EXCLUSIVE: ‘BROKEN COUNTRY’ FILMMAKER WARNS CANADA’S SLOW DECLINE OFFERS CAUTIONARY TALE FOR AMERICANS "By any reasonable clinical standard, you could be discharged from our hospital if you had adequate support at home," wrote Dr. George K. Dresser, an attending internal medicine physician at London Health Sciences Centre. Dresser said Foley has been medically stable for much of his prolonged hospitalization, despite suffering hospital-acquired infections, and argued that conventional home-care programs have failed to accommodate his complex medical needs. "You have been at London Health Sciences Centre because the unique needs that you have cannot be met by existing programs in the community," the physician wrote. Dresser described Foley as "a square peg in a round hole," arguing that the hospital's standardized approach to care is poorly suited to a patient who requires consistent caregivers and highly individualized assistance. The physician also suggested that keeping Foley hospitalized may be unnecessarily expensive for Ontario's healthcare system. "A community-based, self-directed arrangement would in all likelihood cost substantially less than continued acute admission, while delivering far better-matched care," Dresser wrote. He urged Ontario's Ministry of Health to authorize funding that would allow Foley to recruit, train and manage his own personal support workers, potentially ending his yearslong hospitalization. Foley alleged that assisted dying was raised again during a disputed discharge process in 2017, when he says he was threatened with daily hospital charges of approximately $1,500 if he did not accept the care arrangements being offered. POPE LEO CALLS OUT ‘FALSE COMPASSION’ OF MEDICALLY ASSISTED SUICIDE DURING FRENCH HOSPITAL VISIT "I don't want to die," Foley told Fox News Digital, describing his determination to return to his apartment with caregivers of his choosing. Foley also alleged that the hospital removed lighting accommodations for his neurological condition in May 2025, making it difficult for him to receive care and consume food and fluids. Foley said the lighting dispute is particularly serious because his neurological condition makes him sensitive to certain wavelengths of light, including those emitted by fluorescent fixtures. For years, he said, the hospital accommodated his condition with amber-spectrum lighting that allowed caregivers to assist him without triggering his symptoms. But in May 2025, Foley alleged the hospital withdrew those accommodations and began requiring staff to provide care under fluorescent lighting. He claimed the change has made it increasingly difficult to receive routine assistance, including help with eating and drinking, because he must wear large, heavy protective goggles that place additional strain on his already compromised neck. CATHOLIC NUNS SUE NEW YORK, SAY ASSISTED SUICIDE LAW FORCES THEM TO VIOLATE THEIR FAITH Foley said he has sometimes relied on personal support workers from outside the hospital to help him consume fluids and that financial limitations have prevented him from arranging enough outside assistance to meet all his needs. He further alleged that some hospital employees have been instructed not to provide care unless fluorescent lights are turned on, even though he says other staff members have been able to assist him using the amber lighting without difficulty. Foley also claimed hospital personnel began asking him questions about suicidal thoughts again around the time his lighting accommodations were withdrawn. Unlike his earlier experiences, he said he refused to engage in those conversations because he no longer trusted the hospital's intentions. If you or someone you know is having thoughts of suicide, please contact the National Suicide Prevention Lifeline at 1-800-273-TALK (8255). He said he does not refuse to discuss his mental health in general, and is not opposed to mental health assessments or receiving appropriate mental health support. However, he said previous experiences with hospital staff have made him wary of engaging in such discussions, especially because he said medical assistance in dying (MAID) had previously been raised as an option. The allegations mark the latest chapter in what Foley described as a nearly decade-long struggle to obtain the kind of care that would allow him to leave the hospital and return to his own home. Despite his prolonged hospitalization, Foley said he has never given up his apartment, which he described as accessible and equipped with a ceiling lift to assist with his mobility needs. "I have my own apartment. I still pay all my bills," he told Fox News Digital. "The last 10 years I haven't given up my apartment and I have wonderful community [personal support workers] that are ready to start working for me as soon as I get the self-directed funding," Foley said. FAMILY SOUNDS ALARM AFTER 83-YEAR-OLD GRANDMA DIES UNDER CANADA'S ASSISTED-DEATH PROGRAM Self-directed funding primarily refers to the Direct Funding (DF) Program for adults with physical disabilities and Family-Managed Home Care for broader home care services. Under such a model, Foley explained, patients with disabilities would have greater control over choosing and managing their caregivers rather than relying exclusively on agencies selected through the provincial home-care system. Foley argued that this would provide more consistent and safer care, particularly for patients with complex medical needs who require caregivers familiar with their individual conditions. He said his physicians have supported his efforts to obtain alternative home-care arrangements, but he has been unable to secure the funding necessary to put his plan into action. Foley said that the existing system has left him caught between remaining hospitalized indefinitely and accepting community-care arrangements he believes would place his health at risk. "I'm not giving up," he said. "I don't want to die, my daughters know I don't want to die, my physicians have always been very explicit and direct that it's not safe to put me in that type of close model that I need direct funding." In the letter from Dresser, Foley's attending physician, he writes in part, "I am therefore advocating that the Ministry to consider authorizing an individualized, self-directed funding arrangement that would enable you to be discharged from acute care and to arrange and direct your own care in the community. I am very willing to meet with Ministry staff, to provide whatever clinical documentation is required, and to work collaboratively on the design and safeguards of such an arrangement." Before his illness progressed, Foley said he had built a career in banking, worked as a television host and comedian, and even trained as a professional wrestler. He described earning recognition for his work before his deteriorating health eventually forced him to leave his career and go on long-term disability. GRANDDAUGHTER SAYS GRANDMA REJECTED MAID BEFORE LETHAL PROCEDURE, ‘I DON’T WANT THE DEATH SHOT’ But Foley said he has continued looking for ways to contribute to society despite his physical limitations. He is now involved with a project called "Bring Roger Home," which he said is working with a nonprofit organization to raise money for the care he needs to return to his community. The effort also includes releasing music he recorded years earlier, with proceeds intended to support his home-care needs and eventually help other people facing similar circumstances. One of the songs, "Limitless with Limitations," reflects the philosophy he said helped him come to terms with his condition. "Just because you're not the person that you were doesn't mean that the person you are can't be limitless and achieve positive things and goals," Foley said. He also urged people living with disabilities or chronic illnesses not to lose hope, even when their medical circumstances become overwhelming. "Don't give up who you are at your core and believe in yourself," he said. Foley said his ultimate goal remains unchanged: to return home, reconnect with family and friends, and live as independently as his condition allows. His experience has also shaped his opposition to Canada's Medical Assistance in Dying (MAID) system, which he argues cannot be adequately safeguarded when patients face serious gaps in medical care and social support. According to the BBC, Canada’s MAID law, which legalized euthanasia in 2016, is responsible for one in every 20 deaths in Canada. Foley contended that patients should have meaningful access to treatment, disability assistance and home-care alternatives before assisted death is considered. For him, the central issue is not whether he has the ability to end his life, but whether he can obtain the assistance necessary to continue living it. "Even in the darkest times," Foley said, "you can still find a light at the end of the tunnel to go towards." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Fox News Digital reached out to London Health Sciences Centre (LHSC), which operates Victoria Hospital, Ontario Health atHome, the Ontario Ministry of Health, and Dresser, Foley’s physician, for comment but did not immediately receive responses. Cheshire Independent Living Services declined to comment.

articles.title: What happened to Ben Kindel? NHL player suffers 'medical episode' on plane
articles.summary: Pittsburgh Penguins forward Ben Kindel was taken to a Utah hospital Tuesday after suffering a "medical episode" on the team plane.
articles.body:
Pittsburgh Penguins forward Ben Kindel was taken to a Utah hospital Tuesday after suffering a "medical episode" on the team plane, the Penguins announced in a statement Tuesday afternoon.

The Penguins say he is "conscious, alert and in stable condition."

"The Pittsburgh Penguins team plane returned to the Salt Lake City International Airport today shortly after takeoff due to a medical episode involving forward Ben Kindel," the team said .

"Team physician, Dr. Dharmesh Vyas of UPMC, as well as the team's medical staff were on board and immediately attended to Ben. An ambulance was waiting upon arrival, and he was taken to the University of Utah Hospital for further evaluation. Ben is conscious, alert and in stable condition."

The 19-year-old Kindel, the 11th overall pick in the 2025 draft, played 18 minutes and 53 seconds Monday night in the Penguins' 5-4 loss against the Utah Mammoth .

"The health and safety of our players, as well as the privacy for their families, are our top priority. The team will provide further updates when appropriate," the Penguins said.

articles.title: 60 years on: The Aberfan disaster through the eyes of those who survived
articles.summary: It is 60 years since one of Wales' darkest days, when a mining community changed forever.
articles.body:
Few events have left a deeper mark on Wales than the Aberfan disaster.

Sixty years on, the tragedy remains woven into the nation's collective memory, a day of unimaginable loss that reshaped a community and changed attitudes to industrial safety across Britain.

At 09:15 on 21 October 1966, an ordinary school morning was shattered when a coal tip above Aberfan collapsed.

Black slurry thundered down the mountainside, engulfing Pantglas Junior School and nearby homes. Within moments, 144 people were dead, including 116 children, on what was the last day of school before the half-term holiday.

On the 60th anniversary, those who were there share their harrowing memories.

"What I remember was the drizzly rain, it was misty. I rang the bell to start school at about ten to nine, before the children went in.

There was this terrible noise, and I looked out of the window. I could see a wall had collapsed and realised I had to get my pupils outside.

As we escaped, I saw the caretaker rushing to get other children out.

They opened Bethania Chapel to take children who had died, but the first bodies were placed in a shelter in the playground.

We identified them before they were cleaned up, and before their parents were told.

I found that very hard. I remember one little girl, I can see her face now.

Gareth Jones, six, was one of the first rescued

"There was this really unusual sound, like a rumble. Like if you chuck stones across the floor, but it was getting louder and louder.

Next thing, water was seeping through the floor, the walls were cracking and timbers were breaking.

The teacher put a desk on a table, and a small chair on top of that. She climbed on top and smashed the window.

And then she held us up, probably by the scruffs of our necks, to get us out through it.

I am so grateful for her quick thinking, she saved our lives.

When I got outside, I could see a mountain of coal and slurry, with dust and water everywhere.

I ran home, and remember saying: 'Mam, mam, the mountain came down to the school'."

Gaynor Madgwick was eight and lost her siblings

"I heard this tremendous sound, like a hurricane. It was so overwhelming, I knew something was coming, but didn't know what.

Then this mass of black came crashing through the window, hurling me from the front of the classroom to the back.

I woke up to find the classroom was no longer the classroom. The roof had caved in on us, and we were completely buried.

I couldn't see my legs, I thought they had gone.

A pupil in front of me was trapped, and he had blood trickling down his head. Another one was trying to get through the roof to get help.

My head was cut open, and I couldn't move my hand as it was stuck in the cracked wall.

I pinched the hand of a child near me to see if it would move. It didn't.

Then I heard someone shout 'I'm going to smash the window' and saw my grandfather.

I started to cry and will never forget the look in his eyes knowing I was alive.

I'd broken my femur, my leg was just swinging and my shoes had gone.

'I'll buy you all the shoes you need,' my mum said as she greeted me outside.

My parents then ran off to find my siblings.

I was later told Carl and Marylyn had died, and all my friends had gone as well.

"As the teacher spoke by the blackboard, there was a rumbling sound that got louder and louder.

The lights started to sway back and fore, but the teacher reassured us there was nothing to worry about. It was only thunder.

The next thing I remember was waking up and seeing light from the sky because the roof had come in.

I was stuck but awake and could see a dead girl on my shoulder.

There was screaming, shouting and crying, but this got less and less.

This was because the children were dying of physical trauma, the roof and slurry coming in, or they couldn't breathe, they had no air.

I was lucky because I had this balloon of air around me.

The fire service broke through the window from the hall, and somebody saw my white hair.

They started digging and eventually they got me out, passing me in a chain from one fireman to another.

I got out just after 11, and was the last child to come out alive.

Tom Harding, the local grocer, threw me in his van with the cabbages and the carrots, and took me to St Tydfil's Hospital."

"I was at my desk, quite close to the western side of the school that took the fullest impact.

Almost immediately I was engulfed with debris and falling masonry, which knocked me unconscious.

I'm told I was brought out and placed with the deceased bodies and covered with a blanket.

Then someone thought they saw my foot move.

I was evidently still alive and taken to hospital."

"After having pneumonia, I almost stayed at home - but was determined to go in for the last day.

I looked out of the window towards the tip and told my teacher I could see smoke.

He said it was just steam from the canteen, which I thought was odd, because there was no canteen in the infants' school - that was in the senior school.

I put my head on the desk with my book over it - I don't know why, it was just instinct.

The next thing I knew, I woke up and I was under coal, soil and muck.

When I tried to breathe, I just sucked water in, and I had coal waste over my face.

There was lots of crying and screaming, then it went black again.

When I woke up, there was silence, nobody crying, and the little boy next to me was dead.

One of my classmates was walking around and he helped dig me out.

In the hallway, there was a queue of children waiting to be pulled out of the window by a teacher.

There was one boy stood there and he just wouldn't move, he was stunned.

I was pulled out and never knew what happened to him.

Then I found out years later he'd died of a heart attack before being rescued."

Ray Lee lost his only child, who was eight

"I can remember being very, very close to her. She used to do things like comb my hair. I had great hopes for her.

We had breakfast, I went to work, and Anne went to school.

It was absolute chaos there - people trying to get into the school.

There was hope in my mind they may find her. I was walking the roads until 10 at night, just living in hope.

I didn't know for certain she'd died until I saw her in the mortuary in Bethania chapel.

I'd like to have known her for that bit longer, because the eight years went very quickly."

"A neighbour knocked on my door and he was in a terrible state, shaking like a leaf.

He wanted to use my phone to call the fire brigade because a house on Moy Road had collapsed.

As we talked, a lady ran past shouting: 'The school has gone, the school has gone.'

I ran down the road and was taken aback - the houses on Moy Road were concertinaed.

A child was shouting 'help me, help me' from under the rubble.

People were going to him, so I headed for the school.

Lorries were arriving, each with about 40 miners from Merthyr Vale colliery who had shovels and pickaxes.

There were bereaved mothers, and I thought 'What the hell has happened?'

Policemen were carrying stretchers with body bags on them, and I thought to myself, where is God? How did he allow this to happen with all these children?"

"I had been on the bus through Aberfan when somebody shouted 'the school has fallen down'.

I remember thinking 'that sounds a bit silly', but looked up and there was a gap.

If you've ever seen photos, it [the slurry] took the junior school, but left the senior school completely free.

I was thinking something's not right, but then your journalistic brain kicks into gear, and I realised I had work to do.

Not as something you want to do, but it's your job."

"You could just about see the top of the school, but it was totally engulfed by this black mass.

Men worked with shovels, their hands, desperately trying to find survivors.

Every so often, a whistle blew and everybody stopped working.

There'd be total silence while they listened for signs of life.

I was aware of some terrible stories, including of two men who played rugby for Merthyr.

One was Dai Beynon, the deputy headmaster and a big bear of a man.

He scooped as many children as he could in his arms to shield them.

When the room was cleared, they found him still holding them.

And there was Bill Evans - a teacher in Merthyr Tydfil.

When he got back to Aberfan, having heard about the disaster, all he had left was what he was standing up in.

His wife and two children had died, and their home had been swept away."

Jeanette Keane's dad went to find her sister

"I was at nearby Quakers Yard grammar school, and there were rumours something had happened and children had died.

So we went running out, we all just wanted to go home.

My parents weren't there, they were at the school, my father digging.

He had found my sister Edwina and she was alive. But he couldn't get her out because the roof would have fallen in.

My father laid by the side of her. He held her hand and she suffocated."

"I was 11 and remember my dad coming home with my sister Annette's purse and a piece of her dress.

He had identified her in the makeshift morgue in the chapel.

When I asked what she looked like, he said 'as if she was sleeping'.

There was only 18 months between us, we were very close as sisters.

From then on, not having her by the side of me was just an enormous loss.

You're only 11 and trying to understand what has happened."

articles.title: Woman sexually assaulted at fraternity near University of Chicago, lawsuit alleges
articles.summary: The new allegations mark the second case of alleged sexual assault to roil the University of Chicago in a matter of days.
articles.body:
A 19-year-old woman filed a lawsuit Monday alleging she was sexually assaulted at a fraternity house near the University of Chicago in February amid heightened scrutiny of sexual misconduct on college campuses.

The college student, identified in court documents as Jane Doe, sued in Cook County Circuit Court, alleging that the sexual assault took place during a party at the Alpha Delta Phi fraternity house on Feb. 7. It names Alpha Delta Phi Inc. and Chicago Society of Alpha Delta Phi as defendants.

"The grief that this has imposed upon me is indescribable," Doe told NBC News in an interview. "It is the first thing I think about whenever I wake up every day and the last thing I think about whenever I fall asleep."

Doe's case comes weeks after a former Cornell University student claimed in a lawsuit that she was gang-raped at a fraternity party, causing national outrage, and just days after a woman reported that she was sexually assaulted at a party hosted by a different fraternity near the University of Chicago.

The University of Chicago, which does not recognize fraternities as official student organizations, said in a statement that it was "prepared to help the Chicago Police Department" in its investigation.

"These allegations are very disturbing to the University community," said a university spokesperson, Gerald McSwiggan. "The University of Chicago is committed to addressing and preventing incidents of sexual assault."

Alpha Delta Phi's national team said in a statement that it is aware of the allegations and that it "suspended the member involved."

"The conduct described is deeply troubling and inconsistent with our values," it said. "We are committed to the safety and well-being of our members and communities and will cooperate with law enforcement as appropriate."

Alpha Delta Phi's Chicago chapter referred all requests to its national organization.

Doe — who is not a student at the University of Chicago — said she learned about the party on Instagram and had gone to parties at the fraternity house previously. That night, she said, she went to the party with several friends, none of whom are students at the university.

Doe said she was dancing with friends when a fraternity brother approached her. The fraternity brother offered her a shot, which she said immediately made her feel unsteady and lightheaded, according to the lawsuit.

She said she had had only two drinks before she took the shot, spaced out over roughly two hours. She described having the "spins" and feeling as though her "vision was underwater."

"I know myself, and that was not the amount with how intoxicated I felt after the shot that I took with him," she said. "I've never felt like that before."

She added that she watched the fraternity brother pour the shot and did not notice anything "odd."

The fraternity member then directed Doe to follow him to a secluded bedroom on a different floor of the fraternity house, according to the lawsuit. Doe expressed her unsteadiness and lightheadedness, which the fraternity member ignored, the lawsuit says.

The fraternity brother began to make "unwanted and nonconsensual sexual advances" on the woman, the lawsuit says. It says she "lost all physical and verbal ability to refuse" the fraternity member's alleged sexual advances.

"I remember backing onto the bed because I knew what was about to happen, but I just — I didn't feel like I was strong enough to get out," she told NBC News.

The lawsuit says that although her verbal ability was limited, she managed to plead with the fraternity brother to wear a condom, which he refused to do. The fraternity brother then penetrated her "without her consent," the lawsuit says.

After the alleged encounter, the man left Doe alone and unconscious, according to the suit. It alleges that other fraternity brothers initially blocked her friend from going upstairs to find her.

Her friend found her unconscious and helped her out of the house, according to the complaint. She said that she faintly remembers her shirt being on backward when she woke up but that she was not sure how she got her clothes on.

She struggled to speak and walk as they escorted her out of the home, according to the lawsuit. Doe said she slept over at her friend's dorm room that night.

The next morning, Doe found bloodstains in her underwear and went to the hospital, where she reported the incident to the Chicago Police Department, according to a police report. Doe told police she believed the alcohol was laced with something, according to the report.

Police confirmed that a 19-year-old who reported a sexual assault at the fraternity house took herself to Illinois Masonic Hospital for treatment on Feb. 8. Doe received a sexual assault evidence collection kit at the hospital, according to the police report.

Days later, the woman was contacted by the University of Chicago Police Department, which she said was investigating her case. Doe said that university police spoke with her for roughly 30 minutes over the phone but that she has not heard from them since. The university police department declined to give Doe records related to her case without a subpoena, she alleges in her lawsuit.

A spokesperson for the city's police department said it was investigating the incident; the spokesperson did not answer questions about the university police department's involvement in the case.

Doe is seeking a trial by jury and an amount in excess of $200,000, plus costs.

Doe's lawyer, Mike Grieco of Gould Grieco & Hensley, said the aim is to also "ensure that this doesn't happen again, and to help reform" policies within the university.

The University of Chicago has been roiled in recent days by a separate allegation of a sexual assault at a fraternity party near campus. A 21-year-old woman told police she was sexually assaulted this month at a party held at the Alpha Epsilon Pi fraternity house, just off campus. Chicago police said no arrests have been made in either case.

"At the end of the day, what happened to me is not unique, and it's not rare. It happens way more than people realize," Doe said. "There are so many other survivors out there who suffer in silence."

articles.title: Common disorder linked to 70% higher death rate, but medication may offer protection
articles.summary: ADHD medication was tied to a 25% lower mortality risk in a JAMA Network Open review examining nearly 16 million people across three continents.
articles.body: People diagnosed with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) face a roughly 71% higher overall risk of early death compared to those without the condition, according to a new review published in JAMA Network Open. However, taking prescription ADHD medication may offer a protective benefit, lowering overall risk of death, the review found. Researchers analyzed data from 19 observational studies involving nearly 16 million people across three continents to evaluate the long-term effects associated with the condition. DEMENTIA RISK MORE THAN QUADRUPLES AMONG ADULTS WITH COMMON DISORDER The review considered both unnatural causes of death, such as injuries and suicide, and natural causes, including physical health conditions like cardiovascular disease and diabetes. Across all categories, individuals with ADHD experienced elevated mortality rates compared to those without the diagnosis. "We found that people with ADHD face an increased risk not only of death by suicide and injury, but also of deaths by natural causes, adding to evidence that health inequalities faced by people with ADHD are broad and wide-ranging," senior author Joshua Stott, professor of aging and clinical psychology at University College London (UCL), said in a press release. The risk of death from suicide was nearly doubled, showing an 89% increase, while the risk of dying from intentional or unintentional injuries, such as motor vehicle accidents, was 55% higher, the study found. HEAVY DRINKING SURGES AMONG AMERICANS IN ONE AGE GROUP AS OTHER GENERATIONS CUT BACK There was also a 27% higher risk of death from natural causes among people with ADHD. The increased risk of death from natural causes was often tied to long-term health risks like smoking and substance use, as well as executive function challenges that can make it harder to manage chronic conditions, attend doctor’s appointments and follow treatment plans. In one analysis, researchers checked whether medical treatment changed overall mortality rates. Among people with ADHD, those taking prescribed ADHD medication had a 25% lower risk of death from any cause compared to those not taking medication, suggesting that effective treatment may lower some of the behavioral effects and health risks associated with the condition. CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES "ADHD is not by definition a life-limiting condition, as the right support and treatment can help people live long and healthy lives," Stott said. "Our findings underscore the importance of ensuring that everyone who may have ADHD has access to accurate diagnosis and treatment." CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER Despite these findings, the researchers emphasized several key limitations. All included studies were observational, meaning the results show associations rather than direct cause-and-effect relationships. The findings on ADHD medication came from just three of the 19 studies, so those results are still preliminary and based on a much smaller group of people. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ Results also varied widely across individual studies due to differences in diagnostic criteria, healthcare access and tracking methods, while underlying factors such as socioeconomic status and other mental health conditions were not controlled across data sets. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "Our findings provide early evidence to suggest that medication may play an important role in supporting the health of people with ADHD, but this is based on a small number of studies and further research is needed to clarify this link," first author Lucy Corrigan, a research assistant in the University of Liverpool’s Department of Psychology, said in the same press release. "Medication is just part of the story; many people with ADHD benefit from comprehensive, long-term treatment and support."

articles.title: 'Estou deformada': pacientes relatam sequelas após cirurgias estéticas | G1
articles.standfirst: Vítimas relatam perfurações, necroses e cortes assimétricos. Inquérito apura se médicos estrangeiros em pós-graduação atuavam sem supervisão.
articles.summary: Vítimas relatam perfurações, necroses e cortes assimétricos. Inquérito apura se médicos estrangeiros em pós-graduação atuavam sem supervisão.
articles.body:
Enquanto a Polícia Civil apura a morte de três mulheres e suspeitas de irregularidades em cirurgias estéticas realizadas em uma clínica da Zona Sul do Rio de Janeiro , dezenas de pacientes afirmam conviver até hoje com sequelas físicas e emocionais causadas pelos procedimentos. O inquérito reúne relatos de mulheres que sofreram infecções, necroses, deformidades e complicações graves após passarem pela unidade.

Uma delas é a professora Adriane. O que deveria ser uma cirurgia estética no abdômen terminou com uma infecção severa e a perda de parte dos tecidos da barriga. Ela conta que voltou à clínica após perceber que algo estava errado e recebeu a informação de que a situação era normal. Com o passar dos dias, porém, a região operada começou a escurecer.

"Quando tiraram os curativos, começou a sair pele. A minha pele começou a sair. Falaram que era normal. Depois começou a ficar preta", relatou.

Mais tarde, segundo ela, descobriu que o profissional envolvido no procedimento não era habilitado como cirurgião plástico.

"Estou deformada. Eu não tenho barriga. Não tenho coragem de botar minha barriga para fora, não tenho coragem de me olhar no espelho. Eu poderia estar na estatística. Eu sobrevivi", disse.

Pacientes relatam sequelas e deformidades após cirurgias em clínica investigada no Rio — Foto: Reprodução/TV Globo

Cicatrizes e suspeita de mais de um profissional na mesma cirurgia

Outra paciente, Gisele, afirma que procurou a clínica para retirar glândulas de gordura localizadas abaixo dos braços. O resultado, segundo ela, foi uma série de cicatrizes que carrega até hoje.

Ao analisar as marcas deixadas pelo procedimento, a paciente passou a acreditar que mais de uma pessoa participou da cirurgia.

"A costura parecia que eu estava num açougue. Tenho certeza absoluta de que foram duas pessoas diferentes. Uma axila tem um corte e um tipo de ponto; a outra tem um corte completamente diferente", afirmou.

A suspeita ganhou relevância porque um dos focos da investigação policial é justamente apurar se alunos de cursos de pós-graduação teriam participado de procedimentos cirúrgicos sem o conhecimento das pacientes.

Polícia investiga mortes e denúncias em clínica de cirurgias plásticas no RJ — Foto: Reprodução/TV Globo

Resultado desigual e medo de voltar à clínica

A comerciante Thaíse também diz ter ficado com sequelas após uma cirurgia para redução dos seios e colocação de próteses de silicone. Segundo ela, o resultado ficou visivelmente diferente entre um lado e outro do corpo.

"Tenho um corte muito grande e um seio ficou mais redondo, enquanto o outro ficou oval. Está totalmente desigual. Ficou muito feio", relatou.

A clínica chegou a oferecer uma cirurgia reparadora, mas a paciente afirma que perdeu a confiança na unidade depois que outras denúncias vieram à tona.

"Começou a aparecer mais e mais casos de pessoas morrendo, necrosando e sofrendo complicações. Eu estou morrendo de medo de voltar lá para refazer", disse.

'Estou pedindo para alguém fazer alguma coisa'

Para as pacientes que relataram sequelas, a principal preocupação hoje é evitar que novos casos sejam registrados.

"Estou pedindo para alguém fazer alguma coisa, para fechar aquela clínica, para ninguém passar o que eu estou passando", afirmou uma das mulheres ouvidas pela reportagem.

Os depoimentos integram o conjunto de denúncias analisadas pela polícia. Além das três mortes investigadas, o inquérito reúne pelo menos outras 24 ocorrências envolvendo complicações e mutilações associadas a procedimentos estéticos realizados na mesma clínica.

Para especialistas ouvidos durante a investigação, as cicatrizes permanentes, as infecções e os relatos de pacientes ajudam a dimensionar o alcance de um caso que vai muito além das mortes já registradas e que agora busca esclarecer quem realizou os procedimentos e em que condições eles ocorreram.

articles.title: Women hope yearly health checks will improve PMOS diagnosis and care
articles.summary: Women with PMOS say too often they are diagnosed and left to manage the condition on their own.
articles.body:
When Neelam Heera-Shergill was diagnosed with polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) at the age of 18, she feared it could one day stop her becoming a mother.

"I'm never going to have children. That's it, my life is over," she said.

The condition affects about one in eight women in the UK, yet despite its broad impact on health and wellbeing, Neelam, from Birmingham, said she was left with little understanding of what her diagnosis really meant.

It is one of the reasons she supports the decision to rename PCOS to polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome (PMOS) earlier this year, alongside a recommendation for annual health checks to improve diagnosis and long-term care.

The NHS said PMOS, which affects million of women, was a health condition that could affect hair growth, periods, fertility and mood .

For Neelam, finding out she had the condition sent her into what she described as a "rabbit hole" of fear and uncertainty.

Not long after beginning university, she started experiencing irregular and painful periods, thinning hair, weight gain and exhaustion.

"My periods were so irregular but when I had them they were extremely painful, massively fatigued," she said.

"I kept going back and forth to the GP... I went quite a number of times because it was affecting me going into lectures and things because I was exhausted."

Neelam described how she was advised to exercise more and lose weight, but her symptoms soon began affecting her studies, causing her to miss lectures and re-sit exams.

She was eventually diagnosed with PCOS, having "never heard" of the condition before.

"It was the comment of 'it'll be difficult for you to have children, but we'll cross that bridge when we come to it'," she explained.

"It was just dropped in a conversation and I was kind of left to figure it all out by myself."

Neelam was inspired to set up Birmingham-based charity Cysters to help tackle inequalities in menstrual, maternal and menopausal health.

She later went on to have a daughter, which she said was a "really big surprise".

The charity founder said the renaming of the condition, which supporters said was "more representative" of how it affected the whole body, could help improve understanding, but there was still a "long way to go".

"PCOS itself wasn't even understood. So PMOS is also something that's going to be really misunderstood as well," she said.

"If that name change means those conversations come more to light, then I'm all for it."

For many years, Rochelle Lewis, from Wolverhampton, struggled with facial hair growth, painful periods and anxiety.

"I've always struggled with a lot of facial hair growing up, it was something I was really bullied about, so I tried to do absolutely everything I could to try and get rid of it," she explained.

"One of my mum's friends, she was like, 'oh, maybe she's got PCOS'. So that was the first time I'd ever even heard of it, and I was probably about 16."

Rochelle said she first raised concerns about PCOS as a teenager, but felt they were dismissed.

"So I went to the doctors and they literally just brushed it off and were like, 'no, we don't think you've got PCOS'," she said.

The 31-year-old was finally diagnosed with the condition in 2025, a process she described as "frustrating".

"It was emotionally draining, not to be listened to, not to be heard," she said.

Now a mother to a seven-month-old son, she said too often women were diagnosed and then left to navigate the condition alone.

The name change alone wasn't enough, she added.

"So you get told, you get given your diagnosis and that's it... we're just left to it," she said.

"We need to have processes put in place to actually help us."

In July, the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) published draft guidance for the NHS, recommending an annual review for women with PMOS, to help monitor symptoms, treatment and longer-term health risks.

"Recommending a simple annual review is an important step towards ensuring people get the ongoing care and monitoring they need," said Marie Anne Ledingham, consultant clinical adviser for women's and reproductive health at NICE.

The health watchdog said the advice aimed to improve consistency of care, increase awareness and support earlier diagnosis and management, with the final guideline due to be published on 27 January.

Dr Rima Smith, clinical associate professor of reproductive medicine at Birmingham Women's Hospital, said PMOS was "so much more than an ovarian or gynaecological condition".

"It's a cardiometabolic condition," she explained. "PCOS never accurately represented the condition in so many ways. It had never captured the complexity and the fact it is a multi-organ, lifelong whole-body condition."

She added that women with PMOS were often cared for through fragmented services and that annual health checks could involve diabetes, thyroid and menstrual function checks, alongside making sure any treatment was working.

"We know a large proportion of women with PMOS have a healthy weight so it's not entirely weight-driven," she said.

Annual reviews are the sort of follow-up both women said was missing after their diagnosis.

"It's great to have annual check-ups if those annual check-ups are looking at the wider picture of what PCOS is doing rather than the lose weight aspect or go on the pill or eat better," Neelam told the BBC.

"If that bit changes, then an annual check-up is absolutely welcome," she said.

For Rochelle, annual reviews are a step in the right direction but further change to care is needed.

"I think if I was to have had a review yearly, then symptoms that were being missed would have been diagnosed, it would have been able to be looked into, and I would have had a clearer picture," she said.

articles.title: Woman told she had cancer by data-breaching hospital worker
articles.summary: Pippa Boardman says she lost "dignity and privacy" after she was told by an acquaintance she had cancer.
articles.body:
A woman was told she had cancer by a hospital employee who accessed her record days before she was due to receive test results from her consultant.

Pippa Boardman, from Lostwithiel in Cornwall, said she had lost her dignity and privacy through the data breach at the Royal Cornwall Hospital in Truro. She said she did not receive an apology from the hospital until it was contacted by the BBC.

The trust said it was "truly sorry" and "appropriate action had been taken".

It added: "While we cannot disclose the details of individual employment matters, we want to reassure Ms Boardman that we have treated this extremely seriously."

Boardman, who is now recovering well from cancer, said her personal information was accessed by a man she vaguely knew who worked at the hospital.

She said: "I got a phone call at home from somebody I know through the sport that I play.

"This man said to me 'Pippa, I don't want you to worry, but you've got cancer'.

Two days later Boardman was told by her consultant she did have breast cancer.

Nine months on, she said her strong recovery did not undo the damage done by the experience, adding: "I lost my dignity and I've lost my privacy."

Along with Boardman's case there have also been other recent NHS data breaches, described by Health Secretary Yvette Cooper as a disgrace .

Boardman said part of her trauma had been caused by the Royal Cornwall Hospital's handling of the case.

She said: "It really distresses me people can't see just how invasive and intrusive it is if somebody looks at your information and then shares it inappropriately."

She said the trust told her the breacher's rights meant it could not give her information, and it only apologised after being contacted by the BBC.

She said: "It took a lot of courage to complain... and I didn't understand why the hospital wasn't really prepared to engage with me.

"I understand that it's because his rights have to be protected. But I kept thinking where are my rights in this."

Boardman said she wanted to prevent others going through a similar experience.

"I'm in a very good place in terms of my cancer. I'm just in an awful place in terms of what happened and how it happened," she said.

The Royal Cornwall Hospital Trust said it was "truly sorry" about how Boardman was contacted.

It said: "Whilst the member of staff had legitimate access to her records as part of their work, it was outside of their role to contact her.

"This should not have happened and we recognise the distress and concern it will have caused.

"Appropriate action was taken following our investigation which was carried out immediately after Ms Boardman raised her concern."

The trust said it had reminded staff records "must only ever be accessed for a legitimate work-related reason" and it was also reviewing policies "in light of the strengthened NHS England guidance on inappropriate access to patient information".

articles.title: Gaza children face worsening food shortages as prices rise and aid is cut
articles.summary: Families say they are struggling to provide nutritious meals for their children as commercial supplies are disrupted.
articles.body:
Gaza City, Gaza Strip – It has been months since Huda Abu Leila had to resort to serving only tea and bread to her five daughters for breakfast. But this week, that’s what the 30-year-old has had to do, after Israel restricted the entry of goods into Gaza earlier this month.

After living through three years of Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza , and the accompanying blockade that often leaves markets partly empty and goods unaffordable, Huda is used to struggling to provide her children – aged between 18 months and 10 years – with a balanced and nutritious diet.

But the current situation, with shortages of commercial goods, rising food prices, and cuts to humanitarian assistance, has made it ever harder for her to put enough food on the table.

“We were affected immediately. We couldn’t find eggs or milk, and we don’t have the money to stock up on food,” Huda said.

She lives with her daughters in a tent in western Gaza City. Her husband was injured during the war and can no longer work, while she earns a little money by baking bread for other people.

Some days, the family eats canned beans with duqqa – a local spice blend – or za’atar. On days when food is not as readily available, like this week, they dip bread in tea.

What worries her most is how the worsening situation will affect her children’s health, particularly as she is already struggling to provide them with enough nutritious food.

Israel halted commercial shipments into Gaza on October 14, disrupting supplies of food and other essential goods as families already struggling with high prices faced further shortages.

The suspension came amid a dispute over a demand for merchants to pay 10,000 shekels ($3,225) per truck to bring goods into the enclave.

On October 19, Israel announced that commercial shipments would gradually resume.

The Israeli military body responsible for coordinating aid and commercial access to Gaza, COGAT, said merchants had reported that Hamas had withdrawn the demand. Hamas described the payment as a voluntary contribution to a fund supporting people affected by the war.

The disruption comes as humanitarian assistance is also reduced. On October 19, the United Nations World Food Programme (WFP) announced that funding shortages had forced it to cut food assistance in Gaza.

The programme reduced the number of people it supports from 1.6 million in September to 1.1 million in October.

It has also halved food rations, with families receiving one food parcel instead of two, alongside a smaller bag of wheat flour. The number of hot meals WFP provides daily has been reduced from 250,000 to 150,000.

WFP said about 1.4 million people in Gaza, approximately two-thirds of the population, were facing acute food insecurity at crisis levels or worse.

Famine was declared in Gaza City in August 2025. The UN-backed Integrated Food Security Phase Classification said in December of the same year that it had receded after the beginning of the Gaza ceasefire two months earlier.

Families struggle to provide nutritious meals

For Huda, the crisis means she can no longer afford many of the foods her daughters need for a balanced and nutritious diet.

Eggs have become too expensive. A shopkeeper recently quoted her 60 shekels ($19.40) for a tray. She also said some shops appeared to be holding back stock.

Fresh vegetables have also become difficult to afford. When she goes to the market, which she usually does about once a week, she buys only small quantities.

“Onions cost about 10 shekels [$3.25] per kilogramme, while tomatoes cost between 10 and 15 shekels per kilogramme [$3.25 and $4.85],” she said.

The vast majority of Gaza’s population is unemployed as a result of Israel’s war and its restrictions on allowing the territory to rebuild its infrastructure and economy.

The lack of food is starting to have an impact on Huda’s children. She says that they are struggling to concentrate, and often become dizzy and exhausted.

The health of her eldest daughter, Salma, has become so poor that she is receiving follow-up care at al-Rantisi Hospital in Gaza, where a doctor advised Huda to improve her daughter’s diet.

“We have been through so much hardship over the past three years,” she said. “I worry that my daughters will get sick if I cannot provide them with enough nutritious food.”

For Raeda Soboh, 40, the struggle to feed her nine-member family means her children have gone months without some of the foods they need to stay healthy.

The displaced mother, originally from Beit Lahiya in northern Gaza but now living in Gaza City, said her family had long depended on community kitchens, known locally as tekkiya, even before the latest disruption to commercial supplies.

“When a kitchen has food, we eat from it,” she said.

Her children usually have tea for breakfast and a meal from a community kitchen for lunch. In the evening, they sometimes eat falafel, rice, lentils or pasta. But milk, meat, eggs and cheese have been absent from their diet for about eight months, she said. She last bought vegetables about a month ago.

“I don’t buy good-quality things. I buy only what we need and what we can manage to pay for,” Soboh said.

Her experience reflects wider concerns about children’s nutrition across Gaza.

According to the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA), more than 2,800 children were admitted for malnutrition treatment in September, including more than 360 with severe acute malnutrition.

About 3,000 children aged between six months and five years continued to be admitted for malnutrition treatment each month, OCHA said in a report published on October 19.

A UNICEF-supported nutrition survey published in August also found that 12.2 percent of children under five in areas accessible to researchers were affected by stunting, a sign of impaired growth associated with prolonged nutritional and health problems.

Dr Mohamed B Alraee, a paediatrician and nutrition specialist in Gaza City, warned that prolonged restrictions on food supplies entering Gaza could lead to a further increase in child malnutrition, with children already missing the balanced meals they need to grow and recover.

Despite improvements after earlier periods of famine, hospitals continue to receive children with moderate and severe malnutrition, he said. Cases are not limited to children under five, with older children, including those aged five to 17, also affected.

Alraee said some children were suffering from severe malnutrition accompanied by swelling in the legs, a condition associated with serious protein deficiency. He linked these cases to families surviving on a single meal dominated by carbohydrates without enough protein, because they cannot afford more nutritious food.

“Even when the crossings were open and food was entering, we were still seeing these cases. Children do not recover from malnutrition in a month or two. Some cases need three to six months to recover,” he said. “If the situation continues like this, we expect to see more cases of malnutrition.”

For Raeda, the consequences are already visible in her children’s daily lives. She said they had become weak and easily exhausted, leaving her worried about what months of inadequate food could mean for their health.

“They seem to spend the whole day sleeping. When I ask one of them to carry a water container, he might manage it once but cannot do it a second time,” she said. “I feel sorry for him and ask myself: is he getting proper nutrition? Is he eating like other children?”

The family has no reliable source of income, Raeda said. She also said the area where they live is not recognised as an official camp, leaving them without the same aid vouchers and hygiene supplies received by some other camps.

Like many parents in Gaza, she is left trying to meet their basic needs with whatever food she can find and afford.

“I hope someone will help us and stand with us in these difficult circumstances,” Raeda said. “I hope the war ends, the situation improves and the crossings open, so prices can come down.”

articles.title: Why longevity experts are reading organs, not disease
articles.summary: Can your body’s hidden reserves of everyday strength be the key to living a longer, healthier life instead of mere disease management?
articles.body: Can your body’s hidden reserves of everyday strength be the key to living a longer, healthier life instead of mere disease management? That’s how ‘intrinsic capacity’ is quietly redefining conversations around longevity. The concept — introduced in 2015 by World Health Organisation (WHO) — tests how your organs and body systems are performing from the inside out: how briskly you move, how sharply you think, how clearly you see and hear, your emotional groundedness, and your overall biological energy to evaluate your true functional age.
